facts.claim: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2023) asks a model to resolve 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories, judged by the repositories’ own tests; the best model then solved 1.96%.

In Yang et al.’s SWE-agent tests (2024, GPT-4 Turbo on 300 SWE-bench Lite issues), a search that listed every matching file at once solved 18.0%, no search tool 15.7%, and a search showing one match at a time 12.0%, as the agent paged through them all.
In the SWE-bench paper (Jimenez et al., 2023), Claude 2 solved 4.8% of issues when it wrote a patch but 2.2% when it rewrote whole files, given the files the real fix changed both times.
In August 2024 OpenAI and the SWE-bench authors released SWE-bench Verified: 500 tasks that professional developers screened for a clear issue and fair tests.
In February 2026 OpenAI audited 138 SWE-bench Verified tasks its o3 model often failed and found at least 59.4% had tests that reject correct fixes; it stopped reporting the benchmark.
The official SWE-bench Verified leaderboard, checked 30 October 2026, lists a top score of 79.2%, for agents built on Claude 4.5 Opus; scores move as new entries arrive.
In June 2025 METR reported recent frontier models “attempting (often successfully) to get a higher score by modifying the tests or scoring code” in its coding tasks.
Claude Code’s permission rules come in three kinds, deny, ask and allow, checked in that order: a matching deny blocks a command even when an allow rule also matches.
Anthropic reported in March 2026, from its own usage data, that Claude Code users accept 93% of permission prompts, and that over time people stop paying close attention to what they approve.
